questions.title: Question 1: Draw the references (12 marks)
questions.prompt: Draw an empty singly linked list, then the memory after each of `addFront(12)`, `addFront(27)` and `addFront(41)`, in that order. Label `head`, `data`, `next` and `null`. (12 marks)

steps.title: The empty list
steps.body: `head` is a box on the stack holding `null`. There are no nodes on the heap. (2 marks)

steps.title: addFront(12)
steps.body: A node at address 100 with data 12 and next `null`. `n.next = head` copies `null` into its next; `head = n` writes 100 into `head`. (3 marks)

steps.title: addFront(27)
steps.body: A node at 200 with data 27. `n.next = head` copies 100 into its next; `head = n` crosses out 100 and writes 200. List: 27 then 12. (3 marks)

steps.title: addFront(41)
steps.body: A node at 300 with data 41. Its next gets 200, and `head` becomes 300 (200 crossed out). (3 marks)

steps.title: Final picture
steps.body: `head` = 300; node 300 (41, next 200); node 200 (27, next 100); node 100 (12, next `null`). The list reads 41 → 27 → 12. (1 mark)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** The list is 41 → 27 → 12 → `null`, with `head` holding the address of the 41 node. The newest node is always first because each node is added in front.

questions.title: Question 2: Trace contains (10 marks)
questions.prompt: Trace `contains(27)` and `contains(99)` on the list 12 → 27 → 41, using the loop `while (tmp != null)`. Show `tmp`, the comparison and the next reference after every pass, and count the pointer moves. (10 marks)

steps.title: contains(27)
steps.body: Pass 1: `tmp` is the 12 node; `12 == 27` is false; `tmp = tmp.next` (the 27 node). Pass 2: `tmp` is the 27 node; `27 == 27` is true, so the method returns `true`. One pointer move. (5 marks)

steps.title: contains(99)
steps.body: Pass 1: the 12 node, false, move. Pass 2: the 27 node, false, move. Pass 3: the 41 node, false, move: `tmp` is now `null`. The loop condition is false and the method returns `false`. Three pointer moves. (5 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** `contains(27)` is `true` after 1 move; `contains(99)` is `false` after 3 moves, one for every node. With the lecture's loop `while (tmp.next != null)` the 41 node would never be compared.

questions.title: Question 3: Add and remove at positions (16 marks)
questions.prompt: Starting with 10 → 20 → 30, call `add(2, 25)` (25 becomes the node at index 2), then `removeFront()`, then `remove(1)`, then `removeLast()`. Redraw the list after each call and say when `head` changes. (16 marks)

steps.title: add(2, 25)
steps.body: `cur` walks to the node before index 2: the 20 node. `n.next = cur.next` (30), then `cur.next = n`. List: 10 → 20 → 25 → 30. `head` is unchanged. (4 marks)

steps.title: removeFront()
steps.body: `head = head.next`: `head` now holds the 20 node. The 10 node is isolated: garbage. List: 20 → 25 → 30. `head` changes. (4 marks)

steps.title: remove(1)
steps.body: `cur` is the node before index 1: the 20 node. `cur.next = cur.next.next` bypasses the 25 node. List: 20 → 30. `head` is unchanged. (4 marks)

steps.title: removeLast()
steps.body: `cur` stops at the second-last node (20), because `cur.next.next` is `null`. `cur.next = null` isolates the 30 node. List: 20. `head` is unchanged. (4 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** The lists are 10, 20, 25, 30; then 20, 25, 30; then 20, 30; then 20. Only `removeFront` (and `addFront`) change `head`.

questions.title: Question 4: Implement three methods (14 marks)
questions.prompt: In the lecture's `LinkedList` class (an inner `Node` class and a `head` field), implement `addFront`, `addLast` and `removeFront`, handling the empty list. (14 marks)

steps.title: addFront
steps.body: `public void addFront(int data) { Node n = new Node(data); n.next = head; head = n; }`. It needs no special case: when the list is empty `head` is `null`, so the new node's next is `null`. (4 marks)

steps.title: addLast
steps.body: `public void addLast(int data) { Node n = new Node(data); if (isEmpty()) { head = n; } else { Node currNode = head; while (currNode.next != null) { currNode = currNode.next; } currNode.next = n; } }`. The empty list is the special case. (6 marks)

steps.title: removeFront
steps.body: `public void removeFront() { if (isEmpty()) { System.out.println("List is empty"); } else { head = head.next; } }`. (4 marks)

questions.answer: **Check.** For the empty list `addFront` and `addLast` both make the new node the first node; `removeFront` on one node leaves `head` equal to `null`.

questions.title: Question 5: Linked list against array (8 marks)
questions.prompt: State two benefits of a linked list over an array or an `ArrayList`, one drawback, and how an element at a given position is reached. (8 marks)

steps.title: Benefits
steps.body: It is a dynamic structure that grows and shrinks whenever necessary; and no items are shifted for insertions and removals, only references change. (4 marks)

steps.title: Drawback
steps.body: There is no direct access to elements. (2 marks)

steps.title: Reaching an element
steps.body: Keep track of `head`, then follow the `next` references one node at a time (sequential access). `arr[i]` and `get(i)` do not work on the lecture's list. (2 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** Dynamic and no shifting, against no direct access; reach a position by following `next` from `head`.

questions.title: Question 6: Time complexity of the methods (12 marks)
questions.prompt: State the best-case and worst-case time complexity of `addFront`, `addLast`, `contains` and `removeLast` for a singly linked list that keeps only `head`, and prove the worst case of `addLast` by counting pointer moves for `n` nodes. (12 marks)

steps.title: addFront
steps.body: Two assignments and no pointer moves, whatever `n` is: best and worst case O(1). (2 marks)

steps.title: addLast
steps.body: The loop `while (currNode.next != null)` starts on the first node and stops on the last, so it makes `n - 1` pointer moves. The rest is constant, so T(n) is proportional to `n`: O(n) in the best and worst case. For lists of 10, 100 and 1000 nodes the counted moves are 9, 99 and 999. (5 marks)

steps.title: contains
steps.body: Best case O(1): the key is in the first node and no pointer is followed. Worst case O(n): the key is in the last node or absent, so the loop follows up to `n` pointers. (3 marks)

steps.title: removeLast
steps.body: It must reach the second-last node, which takes `n - 2` moves: O(n) in the best and worst case (a list of one node is a special case with no moves). (2 marks)

questions.answer: **Final answer.** `addFront` O(1); `addLast` O(n); `contains` O(1) best and O(n) worst; `removeLast` O(n).
